771.title: The camel's choice
771.hook: every family wants him as guest, and he lets the camel choose, and it kneels near Abu Ayyub's house (sirah)
771.howItsDone: Muslims retell the camel's kneeling from the sirah and Sahih al-Bukhari when speaking of the founding of the Prophet's Mosque in Medina, and honor Abu Ayyub al-Ansari as his host.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Quba, and a Friday prayer on the road. Your line was: the first Friday.

Who gets the guest? That's the question in the streets of Yathrib as the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, rides in. The city has invited him, and household after household wants him under its own roof. In Ibn Ishaq's sirah, one clan after another steps out and takes hold of the camel's rein: stay with us, we have numbers, we have strength, we will protect you. Any answer he gives will honor one family and pass over the rest, on his very first day. Today: the camel's choice.
screen: `WHO GETS THE GUEST?` → `HANDS ON THE REIN.` → `EVERY ANSWER PASSES SOMEONE OVER.`

segments.voice: His answer, as Ibn Ishaq tells it, is gentle and simple. Let her go her way, he says of the camel, for she is under command. So the rein is let go, and the camel walks on through the town with everyone watching. Bukhari picks up the scene from there. The camel kneels at an open place where dates were spread out to dry, belonging to two orphan boys. And the Prophet says: this, if Allah wills, is the place to stay. Then he does something careful. He calls the two boys and asks to buy the land for a mosque. They say, in effect: no, we'll give it to you. He refuses the gift and pays for it. On that ground the mosque of Medina is built, and in the meantime he lodges nearby, in the house of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari. Muslim's collection keeps a small scene from those days: Abu Ayyub, living upstairs, can't bear to walk above the Prophet's head, and asks him to move to the upper floor. Consider what the camel spared everyone. No clan could say: he chose them over us. The choice was left to the camel, which, in his words, was under command, and he passed over no family himself. And once the place was found, he didn't just take it. He paid two orphans what it was worth. Letting go of choosing didn't mean letting go of care.

segments.voice: Think of a small decision on your plate today where several good options are tugging at you and it doesn't much matter which one wins: where to eat, which task to start. Notice your hands on the rein, then loosen them, and let something else choose, the nearest one, or the one someone else prefers. If you pray, you can hand the choice to Allah.
Abu Ayyub. In whose house the Prophet lodged near the spot where the camel, under command, chose to kneel. Today's word.
Your line: let the camel choose. No family passed over, and two orphans paid in full. Until tomorrow.

772.title: The people of the bench
772.hook: poor companions live on a shaded platform in the mosque, learning (Bukhari)
772.howItsDone: Muslims remember ahl al-suffah as a model of learning and of caring for the poor, and some mosques and schools support students who live and study on site.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the camel knelt on two orphans' land, near Abu Ayyub's house. Your line was: let the camel choose.

Too many hadith. Some people grumbled that Abu Hurayra reported too many sayings of the Prophet, a complaint old enough to be answered inside Sahih al-Bukhari, by Abu Hurayra himself. His answer is about where he spent his days. His brothers among the emigrants, he says, were busy trading in the markets. His brothers among the people of Medina were busy working their property. And he stayed close to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, content with whatever filled his stomach, present when others were away, remembering what others forgot. Today: ahl al-suffah, the people of the bench.
screen: `TOO MANY HADITH?` → `OTHERS IN THE MARKET.` → `HE STAYED CLOSE.`

segments.voice: When the mosque of Medina was built, part of it had a covered, shaded platform. The Arabic word is suffah, and the people who lived there were called ahl al-suffah, the people of the bench. Who were they? In another report in Bukhari, Abu Hurayra calls them the guests of Islam: people with no family to go to and no wealth to fall back on. The bench was their home, and the mosque was their school. Bukhari also shows how they were fed. When charity came to the Prophet, he sent it to them and took none of it himself. When a gift came, he shared in it with them. In one long report, Abu Hurayra is so hungry he can barely stand, and the Prophet sends him to call the people of the bench to share a single bowl of milk. Abu Hurayra worries there'll be nothing left for him. He serves them all, and in that story there's enough. The community put the people with the least in the middle of the mosque itself. Not at the edge of town, not out of sight, but beside the teaching. And the poor weren't only receivers. Because they stayed, they listened. Because they listened, they remembered. And Abu Hurayra, who stayed close while others were busy, became the man people asked why he had so many sayings to report.

773.title: "Show me the market"
773.hook: offered half his brother's wealth, Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf asks only to be shown the market (Bukhari)
773.howItsDone: Muslims tell the story of Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf and Sa'd ibn al-Rabi' when speaking of the brotherhood (mu'akhah) between the emigrants and the Ansar, and of earning an honest living.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the people of the bench, poor companions living in the mosque. Your line was: the bench of the poor.

Two strangers, made brothers. When the emigrants arrived in Medina with almost nothing, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, paired them up with the people of the city. Newcomers were given local brothers. Bukhari keeps one of those pairings in the newcomer's own words. Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, from Mecca, is paired with Sa'd ibn al-Rabi', from Medina. And Sa'd, almost at once, makes him an enormous offer. Today: show me the market.
screen: `STRANGERS MADE BROTHERS.` → `ABD AL-RAHMAN AND SA'D.` → `AN OFFER ON THE TABLE.`

segments.voice: Sa'd says, in Abd al-Rahman's telling: I am the wealthiest of the Ansar. I will divide my wealth in half, and half is yours. Weigh that. Not a meal or a loan: half of everything, to a man he has just met, because the Prophet called them brothers. Abd al-Rahman answers, in effect: I have no need of that. Is there a market here where trade goes on? Sa'd tells him: the market of Qaynuqa. The next morning Abd al-Rahman is there. He buys and sells dried curd and clarified butter, small goods, and keeps going back, day after day. Before long, Bukhari says, he turns up with a trace of yellow perfume on him, the sign of a bridegroom. He has earned enough to marry. Neither man is the hero alone. Sa'd's generosity is real and total: he offered half, and meant it. Abd al-Rahman's refusal isn't pride. He answers with thanks, and with a blessing on Sa'd's family and wealth. What he asks for instead is a door: not the money, but the place where money is honestly made. Both are kindness. One gives. The other protects the giver, and keeps his own dignity. The brotherhood stayed whole.

774.title: The charter
774.hook: the Medina charter makes the city's tribes, including its Jewish tribes, one community for defense
774.howItsDone: Muslims and historians study the charter of Medina (al-sahifah), preserved in Ibn Ishaq's sirah and other early works, and some Muslims point to it today when they speak of living alongside people of other faiths.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf turned down half his brother's wealth. Your line was: a trace of yellow perfume.

Clan after clan, written down one by one. That's how the document reads. Medina wasn't an empty town waiting for newcomers. It held Arab clans with old feuds between them, Jewish tribes with their own long histories there, and now emigrants from Mecca, far from home. Any of them could ask: whose city is this now? Who protects whom? Who pays when someone is hurt? The sirah of Ibn Ishaq preserves a written answer, drawn up under the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. Today: the charter.
screen: `CLAN AFTER CLAN.` → `OLD FEUDS, NEW ARRIVALS.` → `WHOSE CITY IS THIS NOW?`

segments.voice: As Ibn Ishaq gives it, the charter opens by naming the believers of Quraysh and of Yathrib, and those who join them and strive alongside them, and declares that they are one community, one ummah. Then it gets practical, clan by clan: each keeps its old customs for paying blood money and ransoming its captives, fairly and kindly. No one is to leave a debtor stranded. Then it turns to the Jewish tribes of the city. The Jews of the clan of Awf are named a community alongside the believers: to the Jews their religion, and to the believers theirs. Other Jewish clans are named in the same way. Each side bears its own expenses. They're to help one another against anyone who attacks the people of the document, and they owe one another sincere advice. And the valley of Yathrib is declared sacred for the people of the document. What kind of unity is this? It doesn't make everyone the same. Each clan keeps its customs; each religion keeps its own practice. It's a one made of many named parts, each listed, none erased. What binds them is a promise: to defend the city together, and to bring disputes to God and to Muhammad, not to the old feuds. Some historians ask how the text came together and when, and the city's later story has hard chapters ahead. But the document itself, as preserved, names party after party and gives each a place.

775.title: The turning qiblah
775.hook: at the mosque of the two qiblahs, the prayer turns mid-way from Jerusalem to Mecca (2:144)
775.howItsDone: Muslims face the Ka'bah in Mecca for every prayer, wherever they are, and a mosque's niche (mihrab) marks the qiblah; in Medina, visitors pray at the mosque known as the mosque of the two qiblahs.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the charter of Medina, the city's groups named one by one. Your line was: one community of many.

A row of people bowed in prayer, and a voice at the door. Bukhari tells it like this. A man who has just prayed with the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, walks past another mosque where people are in the middle of their prayer, bent over, facing toward Jerusalem. He calls out: I bear witness that I have just prayed with the Messenger of Allah facing Mecca. And they turn. Right there, in the middle of the prayer, as they are. Today: qiblah.
screen: `A VOICE AT THE DOOR.` → `FACING JERUSALEM.` → `THEY TURN, AS THEY ARE.`

segments.voice: The qiblah is the direction Muslims face in prayer. In Medina, the early Muslims had been praying toward Jerusalem. Bukhari says the Prophet loved that his qiblah would be the Ka'bah in Mecca, the house tradition says Abraham raised. And the Qur'an, in surah two, speaks of the turning of his face toward heaven, as if waiting. Then the verse comes. In Pickthall's words, in surah two, verse one hundred forty-four: "So turn thy face toward the Inviolable Place of Worship." The same verse says the believers too, wherever they are, are to turn their faces toward it. Now go back to that mosque. The news arrives mid-prayer. Nobody holds a meeting. Nobody says, let's finish this one the old way and start fresh tomorrow. They turn, in the rows, as they are. Bukhari has a second report of the people of Quba hearing it at the dawn prayer and doing the same. Tradition remembers one of these places as the mosque of the two qiblahs, where a single prayer was offered facing two directions. And the prayer's first half wasn't wrong. It was prayed in obedience, facing where they'd been told. The second half was too. What made both halves one prayer wasn't the direction. It was the turning: being ready to change where you face the moment the call comes, without leaving the prayer.

776.title: Badr: the night rain
776.hook: before Badr, Allah sends sleep for calm and rain to firm the ground (8:11)
776.howItsDone: Muslims read surah al-Anfal (8) for the story of Badr, and some recite the Prophet's bedtime remembrances before sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the qiblah turned, and people turned with it, mid-prayer. Your line was: turn to the house.

The night before a fight the Muslims hadn't set out for. They had ridden out of Medina after a trading caravan from Mecca. The caravan slipped away along the coast, and instead an army from Mecca was coming to meet them, at a place of wells called Badr. Now they're camped in a sandy valley, outnumbered, the battle set for morning. A night like that is made for lying awake, running through what might happen. Surah eight remembers what happened that night instead. Today: Badr.
screen: `A CARAVAN SLIPS AWAY.` → `AN ARMY COMING INSTEAD.` → `THE NIGHT BEFORE.`

segments.voice: Surah eight, verse eleven, speaks to the believers about that night. It opens, in Pickthall's words: "When He made the slumber fall upon you as a reassurance from Him." Slumber: a drowsiness that comes down over anxious people and lets them rest. The verse calls it a reassurance, sent from Allah. Then it goes on: He sent down water from the sky. The same verse gives the rain its jobs: to purify them, to take from them a taint of Satan, to strengthen their hearts, and to make their feet firm. Ibn Ishaq fills in the ground-level picture. The valley was soft sand. The rain packed it down where the Muslims were, so they could walk and stand on it, while the same rain made the going heavy for the army on the other side. Some reports add another picture. In Musnad Ahmad, Ali says that on the night of Badr everyone slept except the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, who stood praying under a tree until morning. So the story holds both: a camp of people given sleep, and one man awake on their behalf. Notice the order inside that one verse. It doesn't speak of swords. It speaks of sleep, then rain, and only then of firm feet. Before anyone is asked to stand, they're given rest, and the ground is made ready for their feet.

777.hook: about three hundred against a thousand, two young men of the Ansar in the row, and the Meccan leaders fall (Muslim; Bukhari)
777.howItsDone: Muslims retell Badr in sermons and sirah classes, and the Qur'an's own reminder of it in Surah Al Imran and Surah al-Anfal is recited in prayer like any other passage.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Badr, the night before: sleep sent down for calm, and rain to firm the sand. Your line was: sleep, then stand.

Morning, by the wells. In Sahih Muslim, Umar says the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ looked across at the Meccan army, a thousand men, and then at his own companions, a little over three hundred. He turned toward the qiblah and raised his hands. By the time the day ends, Meccan leaders who had set themselves against the new faith are among the dead, and a small band that expected to be crushed is still standing. Today: Badr, the day itself.
screen: `A THOUSAND.` → `A LITTLE OVER THREE HUNDRED.` → `HANDS RAISED TOWARD THE QIBLAH.`

segments.voice: A very human report comes from Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, the man from the market. In Sahih al-Bukhari he says he stood in the row and found two young men of the Ansar on either side of him, and he wished for stronger men at his sides. Then one nudged him and whispered: uncle, do you know Abu Jahl? What do you want with him? I've heard he insults the Messenger of Allah, the young man said. Then the other nudged him and asked the very same thing. When Abd al-Rahman pointed him out, both went straight for him and struck him down. Afterward each told the Prophet he had done it. The Prophet looked at their two swords and said: both of you killed him. The two he had wished away were the two who went straight for him. Later, Surah Al Imran looks back on that day, and it doesn't flatter anyone. In Pickthall's words: "Allah had already given you the victory at Badr, when ye were contemptible." Contemptible is a strong old word: small, weak, easy to look down on. The verse goes on: so keep your duty to Allah, that you may be thankful. Surah al-Anfal says something close: remember when you were few, counted weak in the land, afraid people would snatch you away, and He gave you refuge and strengthened you. So these two verses tell Badr less as a triumph than as a rescue. The point isn't how strong they were. It's how small they were, and where the thanks should go.
